items.title: Lesson 4 Focus Question: How can you tell from position-time graphs which of two runners is faster?

answer.html: Compare the slopes. The average velocity is the change in position divided by the time interval, ¯𝑣= 𝛥𝑥/ 𝛥𝑡, which is the slope of the position-time graph. The steeper line (larger magnitude of slope) belongs to the faster runner, and speed is the magnitude of the velocity.

Position tells where the object is; velocity tells how fast and which way it is changing position.

items.title: Lesson 4, Problem 43: Critical Thinking, a student skips the sketch and substitutes numbers directly into 𝑥= ¯𝑣𝑡+ 𝑥i for a tugboat heading west. Why is it better to create pictorial and physical models before solving an equation?

answer.html: Sketches and motion diagrams make you choose a coordinate system (origin and positive direction), show which quantities are known and unknown, and show the direction and sign of each quantity (for example, a tug that heads west should use a negative velocity). Without them it is easy to use the wrong sign, the wrong initial position, or the wrong equation. A diagram also gives a way to check whether the final answer makes sense.

items.title: 3D Thinking, Use a Model to Illustrate: Explain how a quartz watch keeps time.

question.html: This is an open-ended research and writing task. Below is a sample short text written for this study set from general knowledge.

answer.html: A quartz watch uses a tiny crystal of quartz cut in the shape of a small tuning fork. When a battery's voltage is applied, the crystal vibrates at a very steady frequency of 32 768 cycles per second. An electronic circuit counts these vibrations and halves the count fifteen times ( 2<sup>15</sup> = 32 768), producing exactly one electrical pulse per second. Each pulse moves the watch's hands one step or advances the digital display by one second. Because every crystal cut to the same shape vibrates at nearly the same frequency, the watch is accurate to a few seconds per month.

check.html: 2<sup>15</sup> = 32 768, so dividing by two fifteen times gives one pulse per second.

answer.html: Evidence: Pepper's line is the steepest, followed by Clover's, then Biscuit's, and Daisy's is the flattest. Reasoning: the slope of a position-time graph is the average velocity 𝛥𝑥/ 𝛥𝑡. Pepper and Clover have the same 𝛥𝑥 but Pepper needs less 𝛥𝑡. Biscuit covers the same 𝛥𝑥 as Clover in a longer 𝛥𝑡 (340 s), so she is slower. Daisy has the smallest 𝛥𝑥 and the largest 𝛥𝑡, so she has the smallest slope.

items.title: Lesson 4, Problem 37: Rank the graphs in Figure 25 by average speed (greatest to least).

question.html: What we know (read from the graph, taking each grid square as 1 m and 1 s): A: +3 to −3 m in 3 s, so ¯𝑣= −2.0 m/s. B: 0 to ≈5 m in ≈3.4 s, so ¯𝑣≈+ 1.5 m/s. C: +2 to −3 m in 5 s, so ¯𝑣= −1.0 m/s. D: −1 to +4 m in 5 s, so ¯𝑣= + 1.0 m/s.

body.html: Speed is the absolute value of the slope, so the steepest line (either direction) has the greatest speed.

answer.html: A > B > C = D (A is the fastest; C and D tie).

check.html: Steepness ordering on the graph is the same (A steepest, then B, then C and D equally steep).

items.title: Lesson 4, Problem 38: Contrast the average velocities of A and B, and of C and D.

answer.html: A and B: A has a negative velocity (about −2.0 m/s, moving in the negative direction) while B has a positive velocity (about +1.5 m/s), and A is faster (greater speed). C and D: they have equal speeds (1.0 m/s) but opposite directions: C's velocity is negative (−1.0 m/s) and D's is positive (+1.0 m/s).

check.html: Their slopes have opposite signs in each pair.

items.title: Lesson 4, Problem 39: Rank by initial position (most positive to most negative). Would the ranking change by initial distance from the origin?

question.html: What we know (value at 𝑡= 0): A = + 3 m, C = + 2 m, B = 0, D = −1 m.

answer.html: By initial position: A > C > B > D (no ties). By initial distance from the origin (the magnitude): A (3 m) > C (2 m) > D (1 m) > B (0 m). Yes, the ranking changes: D and B swap places, because D's negative position is a distance of 1 m from the origin while B is at the origin.

check.html: Distance is always positive, so a negative position can rank higher by distance.

items.title: Lesson 4, Problem 40: How are average speed and average velocity related in uniform motion?

answer.html: In uniform motion the average speed equals the magnitude of the average velocity, ¯𝑣<sub>speed</sub> = | ¯𝑣| = | slope|. The velocity also tells the direction (its sign), but the speed does not.

check.html: Example Problem 3: velocity 1.7 m/s positive, speed 1.7 m/s.

items.title: Lesson 4, Problem 41: Orange and blue cars from point B (Figure 26).

question.html: What we know (from the figure): B is 𝑥<sub>i</sub> = 6.0 km east of the origin A. Orange: ¯𝑣= + 32 km/h, 𝑡= 0.25 h. Blue: ¯𝑣= −48 km/h, 𝑡= 0.25 h.

body.html: Distance from B is |¯𝑣| 𝑡. Position relative to A is 𝑥= ¯𝑣𝑡+ 𝑥<sub>i</sub>.
Orange: distance = (32)(0.25) = 8.0 km; position 𝑥= 8.0 + 6.0 = 14 km. Blue: distance = (48)(0.25) = 12 km; position 𝑥= ( −48)(0.25) + 6.0 = −12 + 6.0 = −6.0 km.

answer.html: The orange car traveled 8.0 km from B and is at 14 km east of A. The blue car traveled 12 km from B and is at 6.0 km west of A (𝑥= −6.0 km).

check.html: The figure shows D to the left of A and farther from B than C, which agrees.

items.title: Lesson 4, Problem 42: Car north at 85 km/h, passing a gas station 2.0 km from the start; position 0.25 h later.

body.html: ¯𝑣= 85 km/h north, 𝑥<sub>i</sub> = 2.0 km (the gas station, with the start as origin), 𝑡= 0.25 h.

answer.html: About 23 km north of the start

check.html: The result is slightly more than 21 km, because of the 2.0 km head start from the gas station.

items.title: Lesson 4, Problem 43: Critical Thinking, why create pictorial and physical models before solving an equation?

answer.html: Sketches and motion diagrams make you choose a coordinate system (origin and positive direction), show which quantities are known and unknown, and show the direction and sign of each quantity (for example, whether a ship that goes west should use a negative velocity). Without them it is easy to use the wrong sign, the wrong initial position, or the wrong equation. A diagram also gives a way to check whether the final answer makes sense.

check.html: In Problem 34, the diagram showed that the answer should be west of A.

items.title: 3D Thinking, Use a Model to Illustrate: Explain how an atomic clock or a CSAC works.

question.html: This is an open-ended research and writing task. Below is a sample short text written for this study set from general knowledge (not from a particular source diagram).

answer.html: An atomic clock uses the fixed energy difference between two states of an atom such as cesium. A microwave oscillator is tuned until its frequency matches the frequency that makes the atoms change state (for cesium this is 9,192,631,770 cycles per second). A detector measures how many atoms respond, and feedback electronics keep the oscillator exactly on that frequency. The clock then counts oscillation cycles; one second is defined as that many cycles. A chip-scale atomic clock does the same thing in a tiny sealed cell of vapor, using a small laser and a photodetector in place of the large equipment, so a portable GPS unit can keep very accurate time.

check.html: Because every atom of a given element has identical energy levels, the "pendulum" of an atomic clock is the same everywhere, which is why it is so accurate.

items.title: 1. Compare and contrast. All four have positive slopes, so all move in the same direction (toward the

question.html: barn), and all end at the same place. They differ in speed: Elsie is fastest, then Bessie, then Dolly, and Moolinda is slowest. Elsie and Bessie start at the origin at the same time. Dolly starts later. Moolinda starts closer to the barn, so she has the smallest displacement, but she still has the smallest velocity because it takes her the longest time.

answer.html: Same direction and same final position for all four, but different velocities: Elsie > Bessie > Dolly > Moolinda.

items.title: 2. Claim.

answer.html: Ranking from the greatest to the least average velocity: Elsie, Bessie, Dolly, Moolinda.

items.title: 3. Evidence and reasoning.

answer.html: Evidence: Elsie's line is the steepest, followed by Bessie's, then Dolly's, and Moolinda's is the flattest. Reasoning: the slope of a position-time graph is the average velocity 𝛥𝑥/ 𝛥𝑡. Elsie and Bessie have the same 𝛥𝑥 but Elsie needs less 𝛥𝑡. Dolly covers the same 𝛥𝑥 as Bessie in a longer 𝛥𝑡, so she is slower. Moolinda has the smallest 𝛥𝑥 and the largest 𝛥𝑡, so she has the smallest slope.

check.html: A start time or starting position does not change the slope; only the change in position and the time taken matter.
